sections.html:
Rochester sits on the southern shore of Lake Ontario, with the Genesee River running through the city. It is the seat of Monroe County and defines 35 neighborhoods, among them Corn Hill, Park Avenue, the South Wedge, Charlotte, Browncroft, Highland Park, Dutchtown and the 19th Ward. The 2025 estimate stands at 206,108 people.

The city grew in waves, with its population topping out at 332,488 in 1950. Much of the housing built for those workers is still standing, so many sellers own a house that is a century old or more. The city's certificate of occupancy inspection checks items such as smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, outlets, handrails and porch guards, and older houses tend to fail on exactly those details.

sections.h2: What homes cost and who owns them
sections.html:
A typical Rochester home is valued at $139,600, yet just 38.1 percent of households own where they live. Renting is the norm.

  • 93,261 households averaging 2.14 people.
  • Typical rent is $1,081, and typical household income is $47,213.
  • Owners pay $1,244 a month with a mortgage and $593 without.

With values this low and renters in the majority, a Rochester seller may be a landlord, an heir to a two-family house, or an owner facing repairs. Those are the cases where a fast cash sale gets a second look.

sections.h2: Winter and the heat rule for rentals
sections.html:
Rochester gets heavy lake-effect snow, over 100 inches in an average year, which is hard on roofs, gutters, porches, furnaces and pipes. City rules also set a heat standard for rentals: owners must provide heat from September 15 to May 31 and keep it at 68 degrees minimum.

If you are selling a tenant-occupied house in the cold months, check the furnace and the heat log before a buyer's inspector does. Buyers in this market look hard at the roof, the gutters and the heating system.

sections.h2: Does a Rochester house need a certificate of occupancy?
sections.html:
It depends on who lives in the house. The city's Certificate of Occupancy program centers on rentals, and its chart assigns each property type a renewal cycle.

When a Rochester certificate of occupancy is required
Property typeCertificate required?Renewal cycle
1 or 2 family, owner-occupiedNo (may be needed if newly occupying)None
1 or 2 family rental, not owner-occupiedYes6 years
Same, in the Lead High-Risk Area or with deteriorated paintYes3 years
Apartment building, 3 or more unitsYes3 years

Rental units built before 1978 are covered by lead-related testing. Fees for permits, licenses and certificates change from time to time, so get a current fee from the city before you budget.

The Building Owners Registry is a city list on which the owner of every building must give contact details, as City Code section 90-20 requires. If the owner is an LLC, the registry asks for the names of the natural persons behind it, a rule in effect since January 1, 2024.

An updated registration is due within 10 days of any change in contact details or any sale of the property. An owner who lives outside the Rochester-area ZIP code ranges, or uses a P.O. box, must name a property manager who is a natural person with an address in Monroe County. Skipping the update after you sell can leave violations or tickets tied to your name.

The City of Rochester bills for itself and the Rochester City School District in one bill, mailed each July. It is payable in four installments, due July 31, September 30, January 31 and March 31. An installment not paid by its deadline accrues interest at 1 percent per month. Monroe County charges are billed separately, and its Real Property Tax Service Office can be reached at 585-753-1125.

State law makes the owner responsible for paying on time even when a bill never arrived. If you sell in the middle of the year, check which installments are paid and have your closing attorney spell out in writing how the remaining ones will be divided.

Rochester deeds go to the Monroe County Clerk's Office, 39 West Main Street, Room 105. The land records page charges $50 for a one-page deed plus $5 per added page, $5 for the TP-584 and either $125 or $250 for the transfer report, depending on property class. A $10 charge on each residential deed has applied since March 11, 2020.

State transfer tax runs $4 per thousand dollars. To get same-day recording you need to be in line by 4:30, and the deed must carry both parties' names and addresses, a full legal description and a notary acknowledgment. The clerk's office answers at 585-753-1600.

sections.h2: Which sale route fits a house that must sell quickly?
sections.html:
An agent, a sale by owner and a cash buyer are the three routes. The condition of the house and your deadline usually decide between them.

  • Hiring an agent works best for a house that is ready to show in a neighborhood with steady interest.
  • Going solo fits an owner comfortable with the disclosure form, the contract and buyer inspections.
  • A cash buyer deserves a quote when the house has open code violations, a lapsed certificate of occupancy, tenants, an estate title problem or repairs you cannot pay for.

With any buyer, ask who takes responsibility for open code violations and whether the sale is truly as-is.

Whichever route you choose, gather the documents a buyer's attorney will ask for. For a rental, that means the current certificate of occupancy and its renewal date. For any house, collect the most recent city tax bill, the county bill if you have one, and a note of the Building Owners Registry entry. If a violation notice has ever been issued, bring the closing paperwork showing how it was resolved.

With those in hand, the closing attorney can ask Monroe County for the right figures, prepare the deed and transfer forms, and file everything at the clerk's office before its 4:30 same-day cutoff.

sections.h2: Selling a tenant-occupied or distressed house
sections.html: Landlords and heirs often sell with tenants in place, a lapsed certificate of occupancy or open code violations. A buyer using a mortgage will want those cleared, and that can take a long while. A cash buyer can take the house as it stands, but ask in writing who is responsible for the violations after closing, and whether the price already reflects them. If the house has a certificate that needs renewing, ask the city what inspection would be required, because the renewal cycle runs three or six years depending on the property type. Finally, tell the tenants about the sale plans early so showings and inspections can be scheduled around the heat and safety checks the city expects.

faqs.q: Does an owner-occupied Rochester house need a certificate of occupancy to sell?
faqs.a: No, not if it is a one- or two-family home you occupy yourself. A rental house needs a current certificate, and a buyer who will newly occupy a building may need one.

faqs.q: What happens to my Rochester tax installments if I sell mid-year?
faqs.a: Ask your attorney. Rochester bills in four installments (July 31, September 30, January 31, March 31), so check which ones are paid and have the attorney set out how the rest get divided.

faqs.q: What happens to my Building Owners Registry entry when I sell?
faqs.a: File a revised registration within 10 days of the sale, since the city requires an update whenever a property is sold. Bills and notices go to the owner on the Monroe County deed record.

faqs.q: How much snow falls in Rochester?
faqs.a: Just over 100 inches in an average year, much of it lake-effect snow off Lake Ontario. Expect buyers to look hard at the roof, gutters and furnace.

faqs.q: Where does the Rochester deed get filed?
faqs.a: File it with the Monroe County Clerk at 39 West Main Street, Room 105. The clerk's office answers at 585-753-1600.
